client: I've been really struggling lately with taking care of my mom — she was diagnosed with Alzheimer's last year and it feels like every week she needs more from me than the week before. I'm exhausted all the time, and I feel this constant guilt like I'm never doing enough, even when I'm giving everything I have. Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the situation isn't going to change.
therapist:
What you're carrying right now is genuinely heavy — caring for someone you love while watching them change, and pouring yourself out day after day, is one of the most demanding things a person can do, and that exhaustion you're feeling makes complete sense. I hear your skepticism about talking, and you're right that we can't change your mom's diagnosis — but I'm curious whether we might be able to ease some of the weight you're placing on *yourself*, particularly that voice telling you you're never doing enough even when you're giving everything. 

What does "doing enough" actually look like in your mind — is there a version of this situation where you'd finally feel like you'd met that bar?

client: Honestly, when I try to picture what "enough" would look like, I just draw a blank — or I get this image of her being comfortable and not confused and not scared, which I know isn't something I can actually give her. So I guess the bar keeps moving because the disease keeps moving, and no matter what I do, she's still getting worse. It's like I'm being graded on something I was never going to pass.
therapist:
That image you just described — being graded on something you were never going to pass — is such a painful and honest way to put it, and it also sounds like your mind has quietly set up an impossible standard where *your success is measured by something outside your control entirely*. What you *can* actually give her — your presence, your patience, your showing up day after day — that's real, and it's significant, even when the disease doesn't reflect it back to you. 

I'm wondering, if a close friend described caring for *their* parent exactly the way you've described caring for yours, what grade would you give *them*?

client: I'd probably say they were doing an incredible job and that they should be proud of themselves — I wouldn't even think twice about it. But when I try to turn that around on myself, it just doesn't land the same way, it feels almost dishonest to give myself that kind of credit. I know what you're getting at, and I see the logic, but there's this part of me that thinks my situation is somehow different, like the rules don't apply to me the same way.
therapist: That gap you're noticing — where compassion flows easily toward others but feels almost fraudulent when you turn it toward yourself — is so common, and the fact that you can see the logic but still feel the resistance tells us something important: this isn't really about logic at all, it's a deeply held belief that *you specifically* are held to a different standard, and that belief deserves some gentle curiosity rather than just a rational argument. I'm not going to try to talk you out of that feeling, but I am interested in where it comes from — like, what is it about *your* situation that feels like it earns you less grace than you'd give anyone else in your shoes? What does that inner voice say makes you the exception?

client: I think part of it is that she's my mom, so it feels like the stakes are higher and the obligation is deeper than it would be for anyone else. There's also this old voice that says I should have been a better kid when I had the chance, and now this is sort of my opportunity to make up for that, so falling short feels like I'm failing twice. I've never really said that out loud before, and I'm not sure what to do with it now that I have.
therapist:
Thank you for trusting that out loud — that took real courage, and what you just named feels like it might be at the very heart of that impossible standard you've been holding yourself to. It sounds like part of you has framed this caregiving as a kind of debt repayment, which means every hard day doesn't just feel like exhaustion — it feels like evidence that you're still not good enough, going all the way back to childhood. 

I'm curious — what was that kid back then actually carrying, and do you think they deserve the same compassion you'd so readily give to anyone else?

client: That kid was carrying a lot of confusion and probably some fear — my mom was unpredictable back then, not like now but in a different way, and I spent a lot of energy trying to read the room and not make things worse. When I think about giving that kid compassion, something in me softens for a second, but then I feel guilty for even going there, like I'm making excuses or shifting blame onto her when she's the one who's sick and needs me now. I don't know how to hold both things at once — that I might have deserved more back then, and that she deserves everything I can give her now.
therapist:
What you just described — that brief softening toward your younger self before guilt pulls you back — that softening is real and important, and it's not a betrayal of your mom to let it exist. Holding both things at once, that you deserved more then *and* that she deserves your care now, isn't shifting blame or making excuses; it's actually a more complete and honest picture of a complicated relationship that has always had more than one layer to it. 

I wonder if the guilt that rushes in when you start to soften toward yourself might itself be an old habit from that little kid who learned that their own needs were dangerous to acknowledge — does that resonate at all?

client: Yeah, that does resonate, more than I expected it to — like there's something familiar about pushing my own needs aside so fast that I barely notice I had them. But I'm also a little wary of this, because if I start letting myself acknowledge what I needed back then, I'm afraid it's going to open something I don't have the time or energy to deal with right now, not when she still needs me every single day. It feels like a luxury I can't afford.
therapist:
That instinct to protect yourself right now is wise, not avoidant — you're not refusing to grow, you're recognizing that you're already carrying an enormous load, and that's actually a form of self-awareness worth honoring. We don't have to tear anything open; in fact, good therapy isn't about forcing doors that don't feel safe, but rather just noticing they exist and maybe letting a little light in around the edges at a pace that works for you. 

I'm curious — what would it look like to acknowledge your own needs in just the smallest, most manageable way, something so small it doesn't feel like a luxury, just while you're in the middle of all of this?

client: I think the most honest answer is that I don't really know what my needs even are anymore, because I've been in survival mode for so long that I've lost track of what I actually want or enjoy. Maybe something like sitting outside with a cup of coffee without looking at my phone for ten minutes — but even as I say that, I can hear myself thinking I should be using that time to do something for her instead. It's like my needs and my guilt are so tangled up together that I can't pull one out without the other coming with it.
therapist:
The fact that something as simple as ten minutes with a cup of coffee came to you — that's not nothing, that's actually your needs quietly making themselves known even through all the noise, and it matters. What strikes me is that you didn't say you *can't* have that time, you said you *should* be using it for her instead — which is that same old voice turning rest into a moral failure rather than something that might actually help you keep going. 

What if, just as a small experiment this week, you tried those ten minutes outside — not as a luxury or a reward, but just to see what it feels like to let yourself exist for a moment without earning it?

client: I want to say yes to that, and part of me genuinely does, but I already know what's going to happen — I'll sit down with that coffee and within two minutes I'll be running through the list of things I haven't done for her yet, and it'll feel worse than if I'd just stayed busy. I guess what I'm scared of is that the quiet will just give the guilt more room to get louder, not less. How do you actually stop your brain from doing that?
therapist:
What you're describing is so real — stillness can feel threatening when your mind has been trained to treat rest as danger, and that fear makes complete sense given everything we've talked about today. The goal isn't actually to stop your brain from doing that, because fighting the thoughts usually gives them more power; it's more about learning to notice them arriving without automatically believing they're telling the truth — something like, "there's the guilt voice again," rather than dropping everything to obey it. 

I wonder if the ten minutes might feel less like a battle if you went in expecting the guilt to show up, almost like you're just watching it do its thing from a slight distance — does that feel like something worth trying, even once?

client: That framing actually helps a little — like I'm not trying to win a fight against the guilt, just letting it be there without it being in charge. I think I could maybe try that once, just to see, though I'm not making any promises because I know myself and I know how easy it is for that voice to go from background noise to the only thing I can hear. But I guess trying once and it being hard is still different from not trying at all.
therapist:
"Trying once and it being hard is still different from not trying at all" — that's actually a really significant shift from where you started today, when you weren't even sure talking could change anything, and I want you to notice that *you* arrived at that, not me. You're not making promises, you're not pretending it'll be easy, you're just leaving a small door open — and honestly, that's exactly the right size of step for where you are right now. 

When you do try it, I'd love to hear what you notice — not whether you succeeded or failed, but just what it was like to show up for yourself for ten minutes, guilt and all.

client: It's a little strange to hear that framed as a shift, because from the inside it just feels like I'm agreeing to something small while still half-expecting to fail at it. But I think what actually helped today wasn't being told to think differently — it was feeling like someone understood why it's so hard before asking me to try anything. I'll see how the week goes, and I'm not sure I'll have anything hopeful to report back, but I don't feel quite as alone in it as I did an hour ago.
therapist:
What you just described - feeling understood before being asked to change anything - that's not a small thing, that's actually the only order in which any of this can work, and I'm really glad it landed that way today. And "not quite as alone in it" after everything you're carrying is genuinely meaningful progress, even if it doesn't feel dramatic from the inside. 

You don't need to bring anything hopeful next time — you can bring exactly what's true, whether that's that the ten minutes helped, or that the guilt won, or just that the week was hard, and we'll work with whatever's real.
